findings.reason: the bound should be raised to cover the population the plan names (it fits comfortably in the stated timeout) or the plan should state a sampling rule and require the fraction, because as written the census can return a wrong answer about a small, biased tail of the manifests it claims to survey.
findings.text: the census caps at "at most 3,000 manifests" over `r-202610*/` and `r-202611*/`, but that population holds 14,204 `manifest.md` files today (a full read of all of them took 52 s, against the plan's own `timeout 600`), so the bound — not the timeout — stops the census at ~21% of the population, and nothing says which 3,000 are taken (glob order would take the oldest October runs). The plan's purpose is to learn how many real manifests change reading before the rule lands; a fifth of them, chosen by no stated rule, cannot answer that, and a partial result reads as a complete one unless the coordinator notices the denominator.

findings.reason: the item should name the test it means (the entry-shape test `_looks_like_a_list_entry_token` / the commit-identifier pattern, which needs no tree) or name the tree to resolve against, otherwise the measurement reported to the coordinator is of the wrong population.
findings.text: the third census item counts "`commits` lines still keep a single entry that git cannot resolve", but resolving a revision needs a tree. `_commit_canonical_id` returns None whenever its root is not a readable directory (promotion_evidence.py:366–378: "a git invocation whose working directory has been removed raises rather than reporting"), and the census names no repository at all. Most of the 14,204 runs are landed and their worktrees released, so nearly every `commits` line — well-formed multi-sha ones included — would read as unresolvable, and the number would measure worktree survival, not the sha-plus-subject shape the clause exists to size.
